readerTitle: Two pet shops, one street: why a subscription is a promise, not a price
caseNote: 가상 사례 (반려동물 사료 가게 두 곳, 이력서 작성 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 구독은 가격을 매기는 방식이 아니라 매달 다시 지켜야 하는 약속이다. 구독 매출은 첫 판매가 아니라 고객이 머무는 기간으로 쌓인다.
misconception: 어떤 상품이든 구독으로 바꾸면 안정적인 매출이 생긴다.

sources.text: 사업 모델의 일반 개념 (반복 매출, 구독, 해지율)

factChecks.note: 이력서 앱 사례는 가상입니다. 실제 기업이나 시장 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Two pet shops, one street
body: Two shops sell the same dog food. Same brand, same bag, almost the same price.
On the first morning of every month, one owner has no idea what she'll earn. The other already knows to within a few hundred dollars. The difference isn't the food. It's how they get paid.

image.label: Two pet shops side by side on one street
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 거리에 나란히 선 작은 반려동물 사료 가게 두 곳. 왼쪽 가게 주인은 빈 계산대 앞에서 문 쪽을 바라보고, 오른쪽 가게 앞에는 주소 라벨이 붙은 사료 상자가 줄지어 배송을 기다림. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A delivery rival just opened.
body: You run a pet shop. Your regulars buy a $60 bag of dog food about once a month. A new online rival now delivers food to the door, automatically, every month.

options.text: Offer your own monthly auto-delivery of food, easy to pause or skip
options.feedback: Dogs eat every day, so the need repeats on its own. You keep the customer without winning the sale again each month, at the cost of handling deliveries.

options.text: Launch a monthly surprise box of toys and treats
options.feedback: It adds a new reason to pay every month. But nobody needs a new toy every month, so the novelty fades and cancellations follow.

options.text: Cut your bag price by 10% to stay competitive
options.feedback: You give up margin on every sale, and you still have to win each customer back every month. The rival's convenience is untouched.

cards.title: Same customers, very different first day.
body: Both shops have 200 regular customers. Shop A sells bags at $60. Shop B delivers the same bag for $55 a month. On the 1st, Shop A starts from zero. Shop B starts with most of its month already earned. Its job is different: **keep people happy enough not to leave**.

breakdown.detail: Every sale must be won again this month

breakdown.label: Sales Shop A needs
breakdown.detail: Each customer could drift to another store

breakdown.label: Cancellations Shop B watches
breakdown.detail: At 5% a month, the number that matters most

cards.title: Subscriptions
body: A **subscription** is when customers pay a repeating fee, usually monthly or yearly, for ongoing access or delivery. They don't decide to buy each time. They decide whether to *keep* paying.

That flips the business. Selling products means winning each purchase. A subscription means earning the renewal, every period, without asking. The first sale starts the relationship. The months that follow pay for it.

image.label: One-time sale as a single coin vs subscription as a chain of coins
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에는 동전 한 개가 손에서 손으로 건너가는 장면("One sale"). 오른쪽에는 달력 칸마다 동전이 하나씩 이어지는 사슬("Every month, if they stay"). 사슬 중간에 끊어질 수 있는 고리 하나를 살짝 강조.

cards.title: Revenue stacks, but only as high as people stay.
body: Picture Shop B starting from zero and signing up 20 new subscribers a month. The only difference below is how many existing subscribers cancel each month. Over time, the shop with fewer cancellations grows to more than three times the size.
cards.softwareNote: Software companies call this recurring revenue and track *churn*, the share of users who cancel each period. A small change in churn moves the ceiling more than a big push for new sign-ups.

cards.title: Subscriptions follow a need that repeats.
body: The model works best when customers would buy again anyway: food for a pet, coffee beans, lawn care, bookkeeping, software used every day. The subscription just removes the effort of buying again.

It struggles when the need comes once or rarely. A wedding planner, a moving company or a one-off repair can't make customers need them monthly. Forcing a subscription there turns a happy one-time buyer into someone who feels billed for nothing.

image.label: Items that repeat vs items needed once
image.brief: 두 칸 일러스트. 왼쪽 "Repeats" 칸에는 사료 봉지, 원두 봉투, 잔디깎이, 노트북. 오른쪽 "Once" 칸에는 웨딩 케이크, 이삿짐 상자, 공구 상자. 왼쪽 물건들 주위에 순환 화살표. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A subscription is an obligation, both ways.
body: You owe delivery every period. A late box or a missed service visit costs you the whole future stream, not one sale.
Customers notice when they pay for things they don't use. If cancelling is hard, you may keep the money for a few months but lose trust, reviews and referrals.
And subscribers often expect a lower price per item. Shop B earns $5 less per bag than Shop A. That only pays off if subscribers stay longer.

cards.title: Now it's a résumé-building app.
body: Your app helps people write résumés and cover letters. Most users are active for three to six weeks while job hunting, then disappear until their next search, often years later.

options.text: A $10 monthly subscription, easy to cancel
options.feedback: Honest and simple. But most users leave after a month or two, so revenue never stacks, and you pay to win every customer from scratch.

options.text: A one-time payment for a job-search pass, say 60 days of access
options.feedback: It matches how the need actually shows up: once, intensely, then gone. You give up repeat billing but avoid angry cancellations and refund requests.

options.text: An annual plan that renews automatically
options.feedback: You collect more up front. But a renewal a year later, for something they no longer use, feels like a trap and invites refunds and bad reviews.

cards.title: A subscription is a promise you renew every month.
body: It turns repeat buying into predictable revenue, but only when the need repeats and you keep earning the renewal.
**Try it today:** list what your customers buy from you more than once a year. For each, ask: would they be glad, or annoyed, to get it automatically?
